sources.headline: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
sources.text: Image source, ReutersByMax MatzaUpdated 18 October 2026 02:10 BSTDonald Trump has blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.The sanctions were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September. But Trump issued an executive order on Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US national interest, prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions.Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Trump's order was "an important and truly historic moment", and that the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.Since then, Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.The sanctions suspension seemed to add further fuel to the fire.Zelensky said on Saturday morning that the sanctions "could have helped enormously" and that the law was "supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end".He pointed to Russian overnight attacks on 15 Ukrainian energy facilities that had caused power cuts in several regions and said: "Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter."Zelensky said it was "important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening" on the ground.The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy by giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the suspension would consist of a 60-day pause to allow for the Trump administration to analyse the impact they might have on the US and global economy.The suspension drew criticism from US politicians from both main parties.Democrats including the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer criticised the move, accusing Trump of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky.A handful of Republicans also came out against the move.Texas Senator Ted Cruz, a Trump ally, called waiving the sanctions a mistake, telling Fox News that there were other ways to address fuel prices, while the state's other Senatory John Cornyn called the move "reckless".North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis called it "beyond irresponsible", arguing that Trump could bring energy prices down by ending the Iran war instead of "doing a solid" for Putin.Nebraska Representative Don Bacon indicated that US lawmakers will now resist funding Trump's agenda.Figure caption, Watch: Will Ukraine get the support needed as tensions with US rise?Zelensky has long stressed the need for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort.He told reporters on Saturday that he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.Zelensky and Ukraine's European allies initially criticised Trump for his plans to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.Trump has spent months grappling with the political consequences of rising fuel costs ahead of the US midterm elections, with inflation souring his standing with the American public.Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.A few days later, Trump claimed that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to facilitate the export of Russian diesel. Both nations have been intensively striking one another's energy infrastructure. Zelensky expressed surprise at the announcement, and said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same. After three days of fresh attacks from Russia, Kyiv resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries.Trump condemned the Ukrainian strikes as a disgrace, but Zelensky said he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests". Image source, ReutersImage caption, Zaporizhzhia was among regions hit by Russian strikes overnightConcerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. Last week, Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield missions, Ukraine said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks. Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that Ukraine had been told by US officials the speed restrictions were linked to technical issues.However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found "these problems do not exist" and the system was operating at higher speeds.Trump has denied deliberately slowing down the network and denied another accusation by Zelensky that US had withdrawn intelligence-sharing.Ukrainian authorities said that at least nine people have been killed and around 60 injured in Russian strikes across the country since Friday. That included an ambulance driver killed and 20 others injured in a Russian strike on the city of Kherson, they said.Additional reporting by Helen Sullivan and Sareen Habeshian

sources.headline: Off the Record: Trump blames Zelenskyy to cover up his own mess in a dramatic week for Ukraine
sources.text:
Welcome back to Off the Record after another hectic week.
I like to joke with our Deputy Head of EU News, Maia de la Baume, that things cannot get crazier with each passing week. Every time, I’m proved wrong. It’s bad news for my immune system, which has finally succumbed to a cold.
This week, I spent some time in Warsaw before the European Council summit in Brussels, which wrapped up as I sat down to file this newsletter next to my Kleenex.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was in Brussels for the summit on Friday, looking to shore up support after a brutal week for Kyiv. The mood in Ukraine heading into the winter couldn't be grimmer.
Fears of abandonment mounted this week after the US announced a shocking deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel in a desperate attempt to bring down fuel prices. The deal is deeply flawed. It gives Russia a fresh revenue boost with no strings attached and little to show for it beyond temporary relief.
By now, it should be clear that President Donald Trump is freaking out about the US midterm elections. Petrol prices have surged since the start of the year, pushing up the cost of living for Americans. Across the Atlantic, the US national average for gas prices hit $4.27 a gallon this week.
If you know anything about Americans, they expect cheap energy – and plenty of it. Prices at the pump and fears of an economic downturn will prove decisive in the midterms.
Much of the pain stems from the collateral effects of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Now, you could argue that Tehran poses a real threat to the world's security and, as Trump himself has suggested, that the country is led by a bunch of crazy people. They are. But they are not dumb.
Iran has successfully weaponised the Strait of Hormuz, choking off the passage of roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil supply. That's a problem for everyone. And someone is going to have to take the blame. Trump has picked Zelenskyy.
Sure, Ukraine is knocking out Russian refineries, hitting Moscow where it hurts and reducing global refining capacity. But that is not the root of the problem. The situation in the Strait of Hormuz is - and Trump doesn't have a quick solution for it.
Instead, the US president has sharply escalated his rhetoric against Zelenskyy, accusing him of creating “problems for our ranchers, our farmers, and the world”. He also suggested Zelenskyy, whom he once described as “a modestly successful comedian,” claims to want peace with Russia while working against it. Ukraine should therefore get a new leader.
This is a shocking statement to make about a country that is surviving daily missile strikes and, coincidentally or not, has encountered serious operational difficulties this week with critical intelligence and infrastructure needed to prevent more people from dying.
Trump has never used that kind of language towards Russia’s Vladimir Putin. He has never called on Putin to hold free elections, either. His words reveal a striking bias that is inappropriate for a country seeking to mediate between the two sides. There is also an element of personal animosity.
The US president has criticised everything about Zelenskyy: his military attire (he now wears a black jacket), his manners (remember the “you don’t have the cards” episode?) and his refusal to budge. Trump’s frustration seems to stem from his perception of Zelenskyy as an obstacle to peace.
Much can be said about Zelenskyy’s tactics, his diplomatic faux pas and the serious corruption allegations involving his senior staff. But when it comes to the war, he is right to stand his ground: the quick deal Trump wants is bad for both Ukraine and Europe.
Zelenskyy also makes a fair point: refineries become legitimate military targets when they help fund the Russian war machine. You could argue that pressure is necessary in any negotiation to force tough decisions – but it has to go both ways. Trump seems intent in applying it in only one direction.
That reflects the US administration’s calculus. Washington appears convinced that the war is unlikely to change much: the conflict has become a war of attrition, the frontline is largely frozen, and Ukraine cannot win back the territories Russia occupies while inflicting brutal damage on civilians. The human cost will go up, but little will change on the ground.
The US also seems to believe – wrongly, in my view– that Putin can be coaxed back to the negotiating table through business deals and economic incentives, and by persuading Moscow that ending the war is in its own interest. But this approach risks fundamentally misreading Putin’s motivations.
Don't just take my word for it.
In 2021, Putin published an essay titled “On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians”. He argued that the two were one people, effectively denying the historical legitimacy of Ukrainian independence. The full-scale war broke out a year later.
For Ukrainians, this is a war of survival – the survival of an independent nation.
Zelenskyy has not budged on territorial concessions, and understandably so, because what is at stake goes beyond a piece of land.
No one has yet explained what would happen after a hypothetical territorial swap, which Kyiv would never recognise de jure anyway. Is the US prepared to offer ironclad security guarantees in return? And what would those guarantees look like in practice?
No country would willingly give up part of its territory – including land Russia does not even control – in exchange for promises that, for now, amount to little more than words. And what would happen to the wider European security architecture, which has gone up in flames as a result of the invasion?
Zelenskyy arrived in the Belgian capital on Friday with a message of gratitude. He thanked the institutions and EU leaders, who he described as “real leaders” in an apparent dig at Trump. But he also showed up with a list of unresolved issues.
Ukraine is heading into a rough winter, with much of its energy infrastructure destroyed by Russia, an urgent need for air defence and billions in fresh funding for 2027.
In his address to leaders, he said the war next year would cost €155 billion, of which €70 billion would have to be financed by the Europeans. He urged them to find the resources, arguing that his estimate is realistic.
Two things stand out. Ukraine is working on the basis that the war will last at least another year, so it has to budget for it. And Europeans will have to foot a substantial part of the bill, with the US no longer providing any assistance.
Last December, European leaders signed off on a €90 billion loan that was supposed to cover two years of financial needs. By now, we know it won’t be enough. And Ukraine will probably never be able to repay it.
The question of financing may be a crude one, but it is a critical one.
European leaders know that cash is tight. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, told me in an interview this week that it is palpable that European public opinion has changed compared with four years ago, as there is an element of fatigue.
The mega election cycle in Europe over the next 12 months doesn’t play into Ukraine’s hands, and the EU should be clear-eyed about it.
In France, Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, used a visit to Brussels this week to send a message to both Brussels and Zelenskyy: she ain’t paying.
On the basis that France is “on the brink of default”, Le Pen said the country could no longer afford to contribute to the common pot for Ukraine. If others want to pay, she said, that is fine, but France won't.
She seems to be taking a cue from the Trumpian playbook: Ukraine is not her taxpayers’ problem. In Germany, the AfD says Berlin shouldn’t either. To be sure, this is a minority position within the EU Council, and it is not even clear that these parties will come to power. But that doesn’t mean they should be ignored.
These parties are successfully tapping into a growing social and economic malaise in Europe. It doesn’t work in Ukraine’s favour. And there is also a legitimate question at the heart of this debate: where will the European Union find €70 billion to €90 billion, potentially every year?
Issue more debt? Tap the frozen Russian assets? Open up the pool of international donors? Use its leverage over third countries to increase their contributions? And what is the strategy behind this massive war effort?
As leaders gathered in Brussels, they instructed the European Commission to come up with options to plug the financing gap by November. Privately, diplomats agree that it will be up to Europe to keep Ukraine in the fight or give Russia the upper hand. But it is not clear how they will get there.
Emmanuel Macron told reporters it was much too soon to talk about €70 billion, but several diplomats told Euronews that Brussels would probably have to raise fresh debt. While there has been talk of reviving the idea of using the Russian frozen assets, it remains a long shot, close to wishful thinking.

sources.headline: Zelenskyy urges support for new US sanctions on Russia after Trump puts them on hold
sources.text:
A policeman helps an elderly woman to walk out from a residential building damaged by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Saturday.
Kateryna Klochko/AP
hide caption
Kateryna Klochko/AP
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters Saturday to speak out in defense of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after President Donald Trump signed an executive order pausing a sweeping package of restrictions targeting the Russian economy.
The White House decision has further raised fears that Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow's escalating assaults with winter approaching. Russian attacks overnight killed at least four people, including an ambulance driver, and wounded dozens, officials said. Ukrainian drones killed a woman in a Russian border region and disrupted flights at Moscow's airports, according to Russian authorities. In a statement on social media, Zelenskyy described Trump's move to put sanctions on hold as unfortunate, but did not directly criticize the U.S. leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days.
"A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote. Later, in audio clips answering journalists' questions, Zelenskyy thanked Democrats and Republicans who backed the legislation and praised its bipartisan support. He said blocking it would encourage Russia to continue killing and do nothing to bring the war to an end. He also added that limiting Ukraine's ability to retaliate against Russian attacks would not bring peace. "Nevertheless, we very much hope — and I personally hope — that the president of the United States of America will do everything possible to make Putin stop the killing, stop the attacks on our energy infrastructure, and end this war," he said. Critics say Trump's decision helps Putin Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling Russia's 4 1/2-year-old war against Ukraine. The bill had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving. Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation.
The president told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details.
Rescue workers walk in front of a residential building damaged by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Saturday.
Kateryna Klochko/AP
hide caption
Kateryna Klochko/AP
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, said in a statement that Trump was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies." "These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said. Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia. Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
The decision has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine — without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump's war on Iran. Kyiv says Moscow carried out a 'massive' energy strike Zelenskyy also said Saturday that Moscow had carried out a massive strike on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country. "The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia's strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences," he said. Ukraine's air force said that Russian forces launched four cruise missiles and 332 attack drones overnight. All of the missiles and 289 of the drones had been suppressed or destroyed, it said.
A car burns after a Russian airstrike on a residential neighborhood in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Saturday.
Kateryna Klochko/AP
hide caption
Kateryna Klochko/AP
Russia's heavy bombardment of the power grid ahead of winter has been an annual feature of the war, aimed at wearing down Ukraine's appetite for the fight by denying civilians heat and running water. Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in the coming months.
Russian attacks killed three people in the Ukrainian city of Sloviansk, Vadym Liakh, head of the city military administration, said Saturday. Writing on social media, Liakh said that two apartment blocks were partially destroyed and other homes damaged. A Russian strike also killed an ambulance driver in Ukraine's Kherson region, head of the local military administration Yaroslav Shanko said. The strike, which used guided bombs, wounded at least 33 others, he said. Ukrainian drones kill 1, ground hundreds of flights at Moscow airports Elsewhere, a Russian woman was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in the Russian border region of Belgorod, local officials said. Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday that its forces had shot down 610 Ukrainian drones overnight over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that more than 100 drones were shot down en route to the Russian capital. More than 350 flights were canceled or delayed at Moscow's airports, local media reported, as planes were grounded in response to incoming drones.
The Kremlin announced Saturday that Russian President Vladimir Putin had approved a government program to help restore trade and logistics facilities damaged in drone attacks.

Zelensky speaks to US envoys amid Trump spat after warning US not to side with Russia

The Ukrainian president said ‘a lot depends on America’ and Ukraine was ready to work ‘constructively’ and ‘honestly’ with the US

Agence France-Presse
Published: 3:31am, 19 Oct 2026

Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky spoke to US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in the midst of his spat with US President Donald Trump on Sunday, saying “a lot depends on America” as he earlier warned Washington not to side with Moscow in Europe’s worst conflict since World War II.

The wartime leader spoke to the US officials as both Russia and Ukraine hit each other’s energy sites, with Moscow leaving thousands without power and Kyiv carrying out the largest drone attack on St Petersburg since the start of the 2022 war.

Trump and Zelensky have clashed as the US leader blocked new sanctions on Russia and struck a diesel deal with Moscow, fuelling fears in Kyiv and Europe that the White House was steering towards Moscow.

After speaking to Trump’s business partner Witkoff and son-in-law Kushner, Zelensky said “a lot depends” on the US position in the war but that “it is clear that there are many things that matter to all of us and that this war must be brought to an end”.

sources.headline: Trump says he's "negotiating Peace" as Russia, Ukraine trade strikes
sources.text:
Updated on: October 18, 2026 / 5:14 PM EDT
/ CBS/AP
Add CBS News on Google
President Trump said Sunday he is "in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," despite the two countries continuing to trade strikes, including one of Kyiv's largest aerial attacks of the war.Smoke billowed on Sunday at an oil export terminal and depot in St. Petersburg, which was set ablaze after Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia. At least one person was killed, and five others were wounded in the attack in St. Petersburg, which sparked fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city's Ruchi oil depot, local Gov. Alexander Beglov said.A logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center operated by Russian tech giant VK were also targeted, the companies confirmed.
Smoke rises above the city following an air attack on the oil terminal in St. Petersburg on Oct. 18, 2026, amid the ongoing Russian-Ukrainian conflict.
AFP via Getty Images
Russia's Defense Ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency Tass that Kyiv was "resisting" Moscow's invasion but could not "change the current course of events."Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a woman was killed and a 6-year-old girl was among at least two other people wounded in two Russian attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said Sunday.
Fishermen fish on the Neva River as smoke rises above the city following an air attack on the oil terminal in St. Petersburg on Oct. 18, 2026, amid the ongoing Russian-Ukrainian conflict.
AFP via Getty Images
The strikes came as tensions between Ukraine and Washington deepened. President Trump has recently been critical of his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and Kyiv's attacks on Russian oil infrastructure.
Meanwhile, there is still uncertainty about the prospect of further U.S. sanctions on Moscow.Speaking on NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday, Zelenskyy said waiving sanctions against Russia would strengthen Putin's war effort. He also said U.S.-Ukraine intelligence sharing had resumed after being "blocked for some period of time."Mr. Trump told reporters late Saturday that they did not know what his decision on further sanctions against Russia would be, despite signing an executive order Friday night waiving planned restrictions, citing U.S. national interests.On Sunday, Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table. Great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations! Signing that document at this time will do that, and I can sign it later, or any time that I want!"
"Perhaps more importantly, Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way," Mr. Trump said.He also continued his criticism of Zelenskyy, again chastising him for "using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target" and alleging "he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did.""He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead," Mr. Trump wrote.Zelenskyy earlier said that while he trusted Mr. Trump, siding with Moscow would be a tragedy and a "historic mistake" for Washington."People want to forget what's going on. But we can't give this possibility to forget, or to change reality, or to change the truth," Zelenskyy said. "We can't compare me and Putin. He's aggressor. He occupied us. He killed adults and children, his soldiers. He's a terrorist. And that's why I hope that President Trump will be very clear with this position."Later Sunday, Zelenskyy said on social media that he had spoken with U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the results of an Oct. 9 meeting between U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams in Miami, as well as "next steps in diplomacy."
People walk along dark streets during a power outage amid the Russia-Ukraine war and dropping temperatures in Lviv, Ukraine, on Oct. 17, 2026.
Olena Znak/Anadolu via Getty Images
He also accused Moscow of breaking Mr. Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warned that Russia planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter.
The Ukrainian government initially said it was observing the ceasefire.Energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions were struck overnight, leaving tens of thousands of families without power, he said, accusing Russia of trying to cause a blackout."America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," he wrote.

sources.headline: How Trump's diesel deal with Russia will impact the United States and Ukraine
sources.text:
Many Ukrainians and Europeans viewed news from Washington over the past weekend as a stab in the back by their US ally. First, President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel, which involves a temporary easing of US sanctions against Moscow.
And later Trump announced an allegedly agreed "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia. Kyiv said the idea had not been discussed with Ukraine, but that it was prepared to halt attacks on Russia's energy infrastructure if Moscow did the same.
'Trump is not interested in supporting Ukraine'
Security expert Carlo Masala of the Bundeswehr University Munich said the developments showed that "Trump is not interested in supporting Ukraine at all, but that domestic US politics and relations with Russia are far more important to him than supporting Ukraine."
He added that the president aims to sway the outcome of the US midterm elections on November 3 through an agreement with Russia.
All seats in the House of Representatives and a regularly scheduled portion of the Senate will be contested in the midterm elections. Polls suggest that Trump's Republican Party could lose its majority in the House. A loss of the Republicans' Senate majority is also possible. Surveys indicate that American voters are unhappy with high fuel prices, and the US president apparently hopes to influence prices through diesel shipments from Russia.Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices?To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Observers, however, consider Trump's hopes that Russian diesel shipments could affect prices in the US illusory.
"The volume is so small that it will have absolutely no effect on prices," Thomas Jäger of the University of Cologne told German public broadcaster ARD.
The political scientist added that shipments planned before the midterm elections would not even cover US diesel demand for a single day.
"The same applies to any shipments that may arrive afterward, if they materialize, they will have no effect on prices either," he said.
Trump's goal, Jäger said, is simply "the story" — showing voters that he is trying to solve a problem that matters to them.
'No concrete military benefits for Russia'
The main criticism from Kyiv and EU countries is that Russia will use the revenue from diesel sales to finance its war against Ukraine.
Carlo Masala, however, does not foresee the agreement with the US having "any concrete positive military effects" for Russia.
He points out that Washington had already temporarily suspended sanctions on Russian oil exports in March this year, shortly after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran.
"Despite the money Russia has and has received, it has no military strategy for making further advances in the Donbas. The issue is more about the political impact and the symbolism of the Americans striking separate deals with the Russians at Ukraine's expense," the expert said.
Another cause for concern in Kyiv could be US threats to suspend intelligence sharing with Ukraine and block the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) program unless Ukraine halts its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Under the PURL program, European countries procure US weapons for Ukraine.Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again?To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
European alternatives to US intelligence
A possible US decision to stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine for strikes on Russian territory would have "dramatic" consequences for Kyiv, Masala said, but European intelligence, particularly from France, could help mitigate the impact.
While French intelligence is "not as comprehensive as American intelligence," the Ukrainian military already uses it to carry out strikes in Russia with French weapons systems.
As for the weapons European countries procure from the US for Ukraine under the PURL program, Masala noted that the program's most important component — interceptor missiles for air defense — has barely been available to Ukraine since the start of the war with Iran.Support for Ukraine across both US parties
Ahead of the US midterm elections, experts point out that Ukraine enjoys broad support not only among Democrats but also among Republicans. One example is the bipartisan passage this summer of legislation to tighten US sanctions against Russia, known as the "Lindsey Graham Act," named after its Republican congressional sponsor, who has since died.
Signed by Trump in September, the law gives the president a broad range of tools. He can impose sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, financial institutions and Russia's shadow fleet, which is used to circumvent restrictions on oil exports. He can also impose punitive tariffs on buyers of Russian energy products.There is broad bipartisan support for Ukraine in US CongressImage: Valerio Rosati/Visually/picture alliance
"Trump may resist, but political forces, particularly after the US midterms, may push the administration in the direction of trying to seek an end to the war by using the tools available," former US diplomat Daniel Fried told DW.
He added that the "Lindsey Graham Act" and the 2022 law banning US imports of Russian oil are "not absolute, but strong barriers against dumb ideas like a unilateral unrequited diesel deal with Russia."
Several Democratic and Republican senators cited this legislation in a joint statement in which they described the diesel deal with Russia as illegal, calling on the US government to "immediately correct" its decision.
This article was originally published in Ukrainian
